candidate: Hugging Face Jobs (huggingface_hub 2.4.0, hf CLI, HTTP API under /api/jobs)
what: Provider-run one-shot jobs in a container on fixed hardware flavors, billed per minute from prepaid credits; CLI, Python and HTTP interfaces.
problem_here: First internet-rental route: a run can use a bigger or second GPU with no machine to tear down, and spend stays bounded even when the local controller dies.
mechanism: hf jobs run --detach --flavor F --timeout T IMAGE CMD; the provider stops the job and its billing at the timeout (default 30 minutes); the disk is discarded; checkpoints go to a read-write bucket mount authorised at creation (no token in the container); logs are retained; price list at GET /api/jobs/hardware.
evidence: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-pricing ; https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-configuration ; https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-training ; https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-manage ; https://huggingface.co/api/jobs/hardware (fetched without a token on 2026-11-11: 23 flavors, unitCostMicroUSD per minute). Vendor documentation only; nobody independent measured reliability; nothing was run.
maturity: Docs examples date from July 2025; client huggingface_hub 2.4.0 released 2026-10-29, Apache-2.0; steady Jobs features through October 2026 (volumes from local folders, attempts, wait, stats); vendor ships an agent skill; no independent adoption figure found.
cost: Complexity: one adapter around the hf CLI (optional package) or urllib for price reads. Money: T4 $0.40/h, A10G $1.00/h, L40S $1.80/h, A100 80GB $2.50/h, H200 $5.00/h; no H100, B200 or consumer RTX. Failure modes: maximum timeout, signal on timeout and behaviour at zero credit are undocumented; bucket storage is billed; automatic recharge removes the prepaid cap; success status does not prove outputs were saved. Attack surface: account token on the user's machine; code and data on vendor machines.
simpler_alternative: Plain SSH to a machine the user already has (no money, no account).
reason: Only rental route found with a provider-enforced time limit by default, a fixed price list readable without a token, per-minute billing and opt-in uploads; the open points need one paid canary before Adopt.
cheap_local_trial: Free and without an account: read https://huggingface.co/api/jobs/hardware with urllib and compute rate x timeout against a cap. With an account: hf jobs uv run --dry-run (free), then one cpu-basic job with --timeout 2m (under 1 cent).

candidate: Plain SSH running the kit's own controller on the remote host (OpenSSH client; Win32-OpenSSH 10.4.0.0p1-Preview, 2026-10-20)
what: Copy the staged snapshot to a host the user already has, run the same stdlib-only expctl.py there over ssh, and pull status, logs and checkpoints back.
problem_here: Second route with the most value for the least code: lab server, second workstation, WSL2, a Slurm login node or a rented VM, with no account, no package and no money.
mechanism: A configurable command prefix (ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ForwardAgent=no host) in front of python3 <kit>/expctl.py launch, status or stop; the remote run directory keeps the kit contract (manifest, heartbeat, metrics, exit); the local side mirrors it with scp -r or tar over ssh; one new connection per call because the Windows client has no ControlMaster and no background mode.
evidence: https://github.com/PowerShell/Win32-OpenSSH/wiki/Project-Scope (edited 2023-06-20: client ControlMaster and background execution listed as not working); https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/openssh/openssh-overview (page dated 2025-02-20: ssh, scp, sftp shipped); kit files expctl.py (stdlib only) and docs/upgrade/BASELINE.md (139 checks pass on Linux). Design inference by this scout; not run.
maturity: OpenSSH is decades old; the Windows port is maintained by Microsoft (latest release 2026-10-20), BSD-style license, available on Windows 10 build 1809 and later.
cost: Complexity: small transport wrapper plus a run-directory mirror; needs python3 and the kit on the remote. Money: none. Failure modes: network drop mid-copy, clock skew against heartbeat staleness, local and remote state diverging, quoting differences between Windows and POSIX shells, kit version mismatch, remote must be Linux until the native Windows launch defect is fixed; a rented VM reached this way keeps billing, so this route alone must not be used for unattended rental. Attack surface: the user's existing SSH keys; nothing new is stored.
simpler_alternative: The user starts the remote run by hand and registers it in external_jobs (already in the kit config).
reason: Reuses the existing controller unchanged on the remote, is the transport that Slurm and rented VMs also need, holds no credentials on the remote and has a free real test on the machine described.
cheap_local_trial: From native Windows, launch a 2-minute toy run in the WSL2 Ubuntu on the same machine through the prefix (wsl.exe -d Ubuntu -- needs nothing installed; real ssh needs an sshd in WSL), pull the run directory back and compare status; $0.

candidate: Slurm 26.05 adapter (sbatch, squeue, sacct, scancel) on top of the SSH transport
what: A launch method that submits the run as a batch job on a cluster the user already has.
problem_here: Users with university or lab clusters; the scheduler enforces the time limit and nothing bills, so unattended risk is low.
mechanism: sbatch --parsable --time=T --export=NONE --signal=B:TERM@grace [--requeue] script; the job id is recorded in the run directory; squeue or sacct states map to run states; scancel stops; time limit and preemption deliver SIGCONT plus SIGTERM, which the kit's run logger already turns into a graceful checkpoint.
evidence: https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html and https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html (version 26.05, read 2026-11-11). Vendor manual; squeue and sacct JSON flags not re-read; not run.
maturity: Standard HPC scheduler in use for about two decades; version 26.05 is current; GPL.
cost: Complexity: four commands and a state map. Money: none. Failure modes: default --export=ALL copies the whole environment, the B: prefix is needed for the batch shell to get the signal, no signal before the end time unless --signal is given, preemption and other exits look alike, site-specific partitions, accounts and GPU flags, unbounded queue waits, accounting may be disabled. No cluster on the machine described.
simpler_alternative: The user writes the sbatch script and the kit only registers the job id in external_jobs.
reason: Thin layer once SSH exists and SIGTERM handling already matches; held at Trial because here it can only be tested against fakes.
cheap_local_trial: Fake sbatch, squeue, sacct and scancel scripts with scripted state sequences (pending, running, preempted, timeout) in the test suite; minutes, $0.

candidate: Runpod Pods through REST v2 (runpodctl 3.1.0, 2026-11-06)
what: GPU containers rented per second from a prepaid balance, with a REST API and a CLI.
problem_here: Cheapest mainstream source of RTX 4090, RTX 5090 and H100 with only an API key; candidate for a second rental route.
mechanism: POST https://api.runpod.io/v2/pods (image, gpu, cloud, mounts, env, ports, startSsh) returns the id and hourly cost; GET /v2/catalog/gpus gives prices; POST /v2/pods/{id}/action with stop or terminate, or DELETE; there is no time-limit field, so a timer inside the pod (sleep N; runpodctl pod stop $RUNPOD_POD_ID) is the only dead-man switch; at zero balance pods are stopped.
evidence: https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/migrate-from-v1 ; https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/pods/create-a-pod ; https://docs.runpod.io/pods/manage-pods ; https://docs.runpod.io/accounts-billing/billing ; https://www.runpod.io/pricing (updated 2026-11-09). Vendor docs; the create-pod field list was read through a summariser; nothing was run.
maturity: Established provider; REST v1 retires on 2026-11-15; runpodctl 3.0.0 (2026-10-15) moved to v2 and 3.1.0 followed on 2026-11-06; Spot Pods are gone in v2; CLI license not checked.
cost: Complexity: a urllib client is feasible, plus the in-pod timer and SSH or log polling. Money: RTX 4090 $0.89/h, RTX 5090 $1.19/h, L40S $1.09/h, A100 $1.79/h, H100 $2.89 to $3.99/h, B200 $7.99/h, plus disk. Failure modes: no provider time limit, a crashed controller leaves the pod billing until the balance is zero, stopped pods still bill volume storage, list filters are silently ignored, API churn, auto-pay defeats the prepaid cap, default spend limit is $80 per hour. Attack surface: injected pod-scoped API key inside the pod, open ports.
simpler_alternative: Hugging Face Jobs (provider timeout) or SSH to a machine the user already has.
reason: Best price and API among machine-shaped rentals, but teardown depends on the harness or an in-pod timer and the API is mid-migration; build only after the job-shaped route has proven the cap and ledger design.
cheap_local_trial: A stdlib http.server fake of the v2 endpoints in tests ($0). With an account: read the GPU catalog with a read-only key ($0); the smallest paid check is the cheapest GPU for 5 minutes (about $0.02, but the balance must cover one hour).

candidate: runpod-mcp (@runpod/mcp-server 4.10.1, 2026-11-06) and the vendor's agent plugins
what: Vendor tool server, local or hosted, that lets a coding agent create and manage pods and endpoints.
problem_here: none found: paid work must go through the kit's controller so that caps and teardown checks apply.
mechanism: The agent calls tools that hit the vendor API with the user's key; a hosted variant runs on the vendor's side.
evidence: https://github.com/runpod/runpod-mcp/releases (4.10.1 on 2026-11-06; the 23 October note recorded 4.5.0 from 2026-10-20). Release notes say failed hosted calls carry an error_class on an anonymous analytics event. The plugin version in the earlier note (1.8.0) was not re-checked.
maturity: Vendor-maintained; several minor releases in three weeks; license not checked.
cost: An agent-callable tool that spends money outside the harness budget; usage analytics on the hosted server; fast-moving tool surface.
simpler_alternative: Keep the guard's ask-rule for paid vendor tools; no integration.
reason: It bypasses the controller, so there is no cap, ledger or teardown verification; the guard should keep asking before any such call.

what: Marketplace of third-party hosts with on-demand, interruptible (bid) and reserved instances, billed per second from prepaid credit.
problem_here: Lowest prices and the only route here with true interruptible capacity; possible later route for cheap exploratory runs.
mechanism: POST https://console.vast.ai/api/v0/bundles returns offers with dph_total; an instance is created from an offer id; interruptible instances are paused when outbid and resume later; each container gets CONTAINER_API_KEY and can destroy itself; API keys can be scoped with category and constraint rules.
evidence: https://docs.vast.ai/documentation/instances/pricing ; https://docs.vast.ai/api-reference/search/search-offers ; https://docs.vast.ai/api-reference/permissions.md ; https://docs.vast.ai/documentation/instances/docker-environment ; security: https://www.cloudsek.com/blog/tophit-part-2-renting-the-attack-surface (2026-09-29, one security vendor, no provider confirmation found). Live prices could not be read.
maturity: Established marketplace; CLI releases on 2026-10-30 and 2026-11-04; license not checked.
cost: Complexity: a urllib client is feasible. Money: prices unverified today; storage billed while stopped, bandwidth billed per byte. Failure modes: no interruption notice documented, a card on file is charged automatically at zero balance, host reliability varies, offers have end dates. Attack surface: untrusted host operators and neighbours (reported scanning campaign: 297 host IPs, 25 agents planted on rented instances), exposed Jupyter or SSH services, full-access key by default.
simpler_alternative: A single-operator provider or Hugging Face Jobs.
reason: Third-party hosts conflict with the brief's rule of never leaking credentials or data to the rented machine, and prices could not be verified; revisit if interruptible capacity becomes a requirement.
cheap_local_trial: none without an account; a fake API server in tests only.

what: Python-defined functions run in provider containers with per-second billing and volumes for persistence.
problem_here: Second job-shaped rental route with H100 and B200 access and a hard workspace budget.
mechanism: modal run --detach app.py; function timeout 300 s by default, up to 24 h per attempt; every GPU function is preemptible and is restarted with the same input; volumes commit in the background and at shutdown; the workspace budget stops workloads at the monthly limit; non-detached apps stop when the client disconnects.
evidence: https://modal.com/docs/guide/timeouts ; https://modal.com/docs/guide/preemption ; https://modal.com/docs/guide/budgets.md ; https://modal.com/docs/guide/apps ; https://modal.com/docs/guide/volumes ; https://modal.com/pricing ; https://modal.com/docs/reference/changelog. Vendor docs; nothing was run.
maturity: 1.x client with frequent releases, Apache-2.0, Python 3.10 or later; widely used commercial service; native Windows support of the client not checked.
cost: Complexity: third-party package with dependencies, and training code must be wrapped in an App file. Money: T4 about $0.59/h, L40S $1.95/h, A100 80GB $2.50/h, H100 $3.95/h, B200 $6.25/h, plus CPU and memory; $30 of free credits per month on the Starter plan. Failure modes: preemption at any time, 24 h cap per attempt, the 300 s default kills real runs, no price API found. Attack surface: token pair in the user's home folder.
simpler_alternative: Hugging Face Jobs, which runs an unmodified command in a container.
reason: Strong provider-side limits (timeout, budget, disconnect stop), but it needs an App wrapper and a package and has no readable price list; a second rental module if users need H100 or B200.
cheap_local_trial: A fake modal CLI in tests ($0). With an account: a 1-minute CPU function inside the monthly free credits ($0 out of pocket).

what: Open-source launcher that provisions clusters or managed jobs on about 20 clouds, Kubernetes and Slurm with the user's own cloud credentials.
problem_here: Users who already have cloud accounts and want spot recovery; not a first route because it rents nothing itself and has no native Windows client.
mechanism: sky launch or sky jobs launch from a YAML task; autostop and autodown run on the remote cluster; managed jobs recover from preemption by relaunching, from scratch unless the task checkpoints to a bucket; max_hourly_cost filters by hourly price.
evidence: https://github.com/skypilot-org/skypilot/releases/tag/v0.14.2 ; https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/reference/auto-stop.html ; https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/examples/managed-jobs.html ; https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/reference/config.html ; https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/examples/syncing-code-artifacts.html ; https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/getting-started/installation.html. Project docs; nothing was run.
maturity: 0.14.x with releases every few weeks (0.13.0 on 2026-07-22, 0.14.0 on 2026-10-05), Apache-2.0, large user base (star count not re-read).
cost: Complexity: package plus a local API server; WSL required on Windows; per-cloud credentials. Money: the clouds' prices plus a jobs controller VM at about $0.25/h. cheap_local_trial: none on native Windows; in WSL only with a cloud account.

candidate: Money cap by reservation before launch (rate x provider time limit x attempts, fail closed)
what: Refuse a paid launch unless its worst-case cost fits the remaining user-set cap; write the reservation to a ledger before the launch call and settle it afterwards.
problem_here: The brief's rule of never spending without a user-set cap, with billing data that lags by minutes to a day and a controller that may crash.
mechanism: Read the rate from the provider at launch time; worst case = rate x timeout x attempts plus a storage allowance; append the reservation to a ledger file; no readable price means no launch; settle from the actual runtime when the job ends.
evidence: Provider facts: per-minute billing that stops at the timeout (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-pricing); price list readable without a token in integer micro-dollars per minute (https://huggingface.co/api/jobs/hardware, fetched 2026-11-11); billing lag (https://docs.runpod.io/accounts-billing/billing); prices up 10% in 12 months and H100 up 29% (https://getdeploying.com/gpu-price-index, third-party tracker, week of 2026-11-09). The pattern is this scout's design inference; not measured.
cost: Small stdlib code plus a ledger file; over-reserves when runs finish early; cannot bound storage or bandwidth charges exactly; a crash between reserve and launch leaves a reservation to reconcile.
simpler_alternative: Rely on the prepaid balance alone (hard only with auto-recharge off; gives no per-run or per-loop limit).
reason: The only cap that holds without trusting after-the-fact billing; pure stdlib, lives in the remote module and can share the unattended loop's limit ledger.
cheap_local_trial: Unit test with a fake price table and a fake clock: launch refused at the cap, on a missing price, and reconciled after a simulated crash between reserve and launch; minutes, $0.

candidate: Provider-side stop as an admission rule for rental routes (job timeout, remote autostop or in-instance timer; prepaid balance with auto-recharge off as backstop)
what: Admit a rental route only if something outside the user's machine stops the billing.
problem_here: The brief's 12-hour unattended worst case (no job left billing) when the local controller or machine dies.
mechanism: Job-shaped routes: always pass an explicit provider timeout. Machine-shaped routes: start a self-stop timer inside the instance at boot with the instance-scoped key. Setup check: tell the user to keep auto-recharge off and the balance small.
evidence: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-pricing (job and billing stop at the timeout); https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/reference/auto-stop.html (autostop runs on the remote cluster); https://docs.runpod.io/pods/manage-pods (in-pod sleep and stop example); https://docs.vast.ai/documentation/instances/docker-environment (destroy from within); https://github.com/dstackai/dstack/releases/tag/0.22.6 (server crash can orphan resources); auto-recharge: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/billing , https://docs.runpod.io/accounts-billing/billing , https://docs.vast.ai/documentation/instances/pricing. Vendor docs; nothing was run.
maturity: n/a (design rule); each mechanism is documented by its provider.
cost: In-instance timers need the instance-scoped key and fail silently if the start command fails; a fixed timer cuts off long runs unless extended; the prepaid backstop depends on a setting only the user can check.
simpler_alternative: The local controller polls and tears down, which fails exactly when the controller dies.
reason: Turns the 12-hour worst case into a provider-side guarantee and is the property that separates the routes.
cheap_local_trial: Fake provider in tests: kill the controller mid-run, assert that the fake job ends at its timeout and that the next status call reconciles the run; minutes, $0.

candidate: Teardown verified by recorded IDs and labels
what: Record every created job or instance ID and a run label before anything else; after stop, list the provider's resources and require that none of the recorded ones is active; never act on IDs the harness did not create.
problem_here: The brief's rule of always cleaning up what the harness started, without deleting someone else's work.
mechanism: The ID is written to the run directory at creation; the remote job carries a label with the run id; verification lists and matches on the client side because server-side list filters can be ignored.
evidence: https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/migrate-from-v1 (unknown query parameters are silently ignored and the call returns every pod); https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-manage (labels and status filters); https://github.com/skypilot-org/skypilot/releases (0.14.0: fixed leaked allocations on terminate). The pattern is a design inference; not run.
cost: Small; one extra list call per stop; a crash between the provider's create response and the local write leaves an unrecorded resource, so the label is the second way to find it.
simpler_alternative: Trust the stop call's return value.
reason: Cleanup that is not checked is the documented way resources leak, and matching only own IDs protects other work in the same account.
cheap_local_trial: Fake provider that ignores list filters and holds a foreign job: assert that only the harness's own IDs are stopped and that a leftover is reported; minutes, $0.

candidate: Stdlib fakes for remote-route tests (fake CLI executables and an http.server fake API)
what: Fake hf, ssh, scp, sbatch, squeue, sacct and scancel programs and a fake REST server, with failure injection.
problem_here: The module must be testable on Windows, WSL and Linux with no account, network or money.
mechanism: The module takes each executable from config; tests point it at a Python fake that keeps jobs as JSON files and replays scripted states (timeout, error, vanished job, HTTP 5xx, missing price).
evidence: Kit baseline: the existing 139 stdlib checks already test the controller against local processes (docs/upgrade/BASELINE.md). Limit: fakes miss provider drift such as the REST v1 retirement on 2026-11-15 (https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/migrate-from-v1). Design inference; not run.
cost: The fake must be kept in step with the real CLI output; on Windows the fake must be started as python fake.py, not as a bare script on PATH.
simpler_alternative: Mock subprocess in unit tests only (misses argument quoting and Windows process behaviour).
reason: Gives the optional module the same offline test standard as the core; a paid canary still has to cover drift.
cheap_local_trial: Write the fake hf with run, inspect, logs, cancel and hardware, then run the module's launch, watch and stop cycle on Windows and WSL; minutes, $0.

candidate: Final frozen evaluation on the user's machine after checkpoint pull
what: Remote machines train; the frozen evaluator scores pulled checkpoints locally and the held-out set is never uploaded.
problem_here: Goal 1 lets harness code and a frozen evaluator decide what is kept; on a rented machine the agent's own code controls the environment that would compute the score, and data placed there is exposed.
mechanism: The remote job writes checkpoints and its own validation metrics; the local controller pulls best and last and runs the frozen evaluation; remote metrics are advisory.
evidence: No external measurement found. Design inference from the brief (docs/upgrade/scout/brief.md) and from provider facts that disks and hosts are provider-controlled (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-manage ; https://www.cloudsek.com/blog/tophit-part-2-renting-the-attack-surface).
cost: Local GPU time for evaluation, checkpoint download time and bandwidth; models that do not fit the local 32 GB GPU cannot be evaluated locally.
